text: Nier Replicant, Nier Gestalt, Nier The State of Western JRPG Localization circa 2010 was absolutely grim. Square Enix apparently decided the Xbox demographic, and the American demographic for all systems for that matter, couldn't identify with a Japanese teenager experiencing existential despair, so they replaced him with a 47-year-old divorced transmission mechanic whose forehead resembles a GM bellhousing. T56 on the garage floor. 4L60E slipping into third. S10 outside on blocks since 2009. Dad nowhere to be found. Fentanyl afoot. The scum are legion. Meanwhile Japanese players got a young man contemplating the ontological implications of his sister's mortality, the collapse of human civilization, and the metaphysical distinction between soul and consciousness. Americans got a guy who looks like he owes Snap-on $8,400. Same Game. Same existential themes. Just a fundamentally different understanding of the target consumer. And somehow this was considered good market segmentation. The Absolute State of Gaming.

text: Nocturne is one of the best games this year And no.. not the SMT Nocturne. Anyways, it first caught my attention from the amazing reviews it got, currently sitting at 98% positive. After finishing myself, I have to say.. it's pretty deserved. Gameplay What mainly sets it apart is that it's a Rhythm RPG where you beat enemies by clearing the song without dying. For the most part, it is a 4 wide grid where you hit falling notes. I played a ton of osu! mania back in the day and it felt great once I got into it. It incorporates various mechanics to spice it up like building up energy to attack the enemy to stun/block them and you have equipment/items that can give you some advantages in certain aspects/conditions, but make no mistake that the Rhythm aspect is front and center above all else. As long as you're hitting those notes, you're winning (..most of the time). I didn't know how to feel about it at first, but I do think keeping that the focus was the right decision. The music itself also greatly enhances it, with very climatic feeling boss fights. It isn't super out of place either as sound is a core aspect of the game. It may also sound like doing that over its 15-20 hour playtime would be repetitive, but it does a lot, and I mean a lot to keep it varied. Tons of enemies have gimmicks and/or mess with the board. That doesn't mean there aren't a few points where you'd feel it be a little tiring, but for the most part it stays interesting all throughout as you don't know what it'll throw at you generally. While it is mostly linear, the areas are very well designed and look gorgeous to boot. No complex puzzles or anything, just some areas needing you to unlock a door/path. I do think some areas are just a tad too large, and it feels like you move just a bit slower than necessary, but didn't bother me that much in the long run. I wasn't really feeling it in the first 1-2 hours, but it only got better from there. Quick note on the visuals, but it's amazing nearly all around. The character animations and portraits especially.. maybe among some of the best in its style from their incredible detail. Even every single NPC has a unique portrait. It's no wonder it was 10 years in the making, it was pure passion. Story What brings this all together though.. is its story. Now, while it doesn't do anything especially groundbreaking, its execution is fantastic. To say that it's an emotional rollercoaster would be an understatement. I've seen some people compare it to One Shot, but it hits a lot of similar themes to Xenoblade 2/3 and Expedition 33. It explores the concept of a digital afterlife, and pretty damn well at that. Not exactly full encompassing, but a very effective personal journey. It takes a lot these days for a game to make me tear up, let alone cry. This was.. the first game in a long time where I had to actually hold myself back from full on crying (so.. since mystery dungeon). I was not ready for how hard certain parts hit. There are maybe a few aspects that could've used a bit more attention, but it doesn't at all take away from the overall delivery. But yea, in short, it's.. hard to really find much wrong with the game outside nitpicks or wanting it to be something it's not. It definitely isn't for everyone of course, but I think it is a must-try for anyone that thinks they'll enjoy it. It's about as solid as a 9/10 can get. Even if you're not a rhythm game player, its got difficulty options to accommodate, and even accessibility options that can autoplay certain columns for you. There's something special about experiencing the gameplay and story together though which is what I think truly elevates it, as you likely won't find much else like it.

text: Tactics Orge vs Final Fantasy Tactics. Which to play first. Just picked up these two on sale and as soon as I finish Octopath 0 I want to play 1 of them but not sure which one to start with. I might not play the other for a while since I try to vary the games I play. I did do a little research of other posts here but I avoided reading too deep into it since I wanted to avoid spoilers. Additionally, a lot of the time the response was 'you need to tell us what other games you played and what you liked about them' hence why I decided to start my own thread. What I like/dislike in Game's I've Previously Played: The main tactics games I've previously played and liked are are Triangle Strategy and Final Fantasy Tactics Advanced and also Stella Glow. The main thing I liked about Triangle Strategy was that the number of recruits and their abilities were fixed and very well defined. Hence a lot of the strategy came down to picking the right 8~10 characters for each mission. I really do NOT like where you can recruit and infinite number of infinitly customizable characters. Like I tried to play Disgaea and just had to stop since I found recruitment so confusing in that game. I also really liked that TS had systems in place to power level the weaker characters since it allowed me to use everyone more freely. I don't mind where they do a Job and Sub Job system like FFT Adv but again, I found the idea of being able to recruit an infinite number of the same role so distasteful I placed a self imposed rule on myself that I had to have every Job covered and no two characters on my entire team could ever share a Job or Sub Job thereby forcing every character to be unique. The main reason I did this is because otherwise I likely would have just picked the 1 or 2 best classes and had 6~8 copies of those which sounds pretty boring. I guess if I had to summarize it, I like picking a different team of 8~10 characters from a large pool of unique characters that I can optimize for each mission. I don't like the idea of having 1 team of 8~10 that I use for every mission. Hence one question I do want answered is how exactly is recruitment, skills and leveling handled in each game? Difficulty Another thing I'll note is, I hate modern game design that seems to be afraid to let player's fail. So often it's clear that devs want their players to be able to win no matter what team is picked so they make fights really easy. Than when a team that's actually optimized comes along it's a curb stomp. For example, in Triangle Strategy, I did my final run on the hardest difficulty with a Deathless and Itemless rule since anything else wouldn't have been a joke. It didn't help that the Triangle Strategy AI was really bad and couldn't handle some cheesy tactics. That being said, I also don't like devs who mix up 'harder fights' with 'longer fights.' Giving the enemy say 3x hp might make the game harder in a technical sense but in a practical sense it's not adding anything substantial to the game and just making things more annoying. Question two is thusly which game is harder and is it real difficulty or artificial difficulty? Story Not important for picking since I'm sure that both games have a good story though again I want to avoid spoilers. That being said I have heard that Ogre has multiple endings so I guess I should ask if Ogre has a NG+ or if I would need to replay Ogre from the start to see all endings. I didn't mind TS's multiple endings since it was more NG+ and I could zoom through dialog I'd already seen. Experience with Both Franchises As previously mentioned I played FFT Adv and really liked it. As for Ogre, I did play Ogre Battle 64 though stopped about halfway through because... well... I got annoyed that all my units started feeling the exact same and then when I read about the Good-Evil alignment system, the whole thing seems so pointlessly convoluted that it turned me off from continuing. That about sums it up. Any advice or insight would be appreciated. Thank you.

text: Romancing SaGa 1 Minstrel Song Review Bottom Line Up Front Romancing SaGa 1 (Minstrel Song Remaster to be exact) has a reputation for being overly complex in some respects and ultimately I think that reputation is well earned. It has a wealth of mechanics and peculiar hurdles that can really diminish the potential for fun but despite that provides an endearing experience worth a playthrough or two. This was a great leap beyond SaGa 3 (FFL3) but in doing so leapt a bit far off the target zone. Even the remaster does not quite align into a fully refined experience so leaves some opportunities for yet another remake in the future. This game has various ways of trying to bring a tabletop experience like Dungeons & Dragons to the JRPG context but it stumbles a bit out of the gate on that. Ultimately it is still worth experiencing with a lot to enjoy. Details Disclaimer I played this game as its Remastered version on my steamdeck. This version is based on the PS2 versions and updated with various bits. Additional characters (which I didn't really experience), enhanced newgame+, challenging superbosses, and some turbo modes that definitely speed things up (a good thing). This review is based on my first playthrough as Hawke and my second playthrough as Albert. This was supplemented with a few aborted runs with other characters to experience their introductory situations. I make various comparisons to Emerald Beyond, because that game is the closest to this one, compared to the other games I've reviewed in the series.
